turns.text: All right. Good afternoon. My name is Andrew Riggie. I am the Executive Director of the New York City Hospitality Alliance. We’re a non-for-profit association representing restaurants and bars throughout the five boroughs of New York City. Now, something bad is happening in our industry. Back in 2014, there was almost seven percent consecutive annual employment growth. Fast forward today, or I should say the end of 2018, it dropped to minus, almost minus two percent growth and this is since the increase of the tip-wage has doubled. There are a lot fundamental changes going on, and that’s why we need business reform. On today’s bill, 1466, which would create a regulatory review panel. We support this bill. Years back, under the last administration, there were similar legislation that was passed. All of the regulatory agencies were required to review the fines and violations they issued to small businesses. They came back unfortunately with almost nothing. Even the Department of Health, which was mentioned before, out of the countless violations they issue restaurants, couldn’t find one, not one violation to say we’ll provide you an opportunity to cure. So we hope this legislation gets passed, and we also hope that it has the teeth to ensure that all the different agencies come back to the table with meaningful cure periods and warnings before monetary penalties are issued. We also support the compilation of all the rules and laws governing small businesses. We think this would be helpful so we are supportive. Further, we would like to see Intro 408 which would provide affordable rent for commercial establishments in certain development spaces. We think this would go a long way in help preserving some of our small businesses, however, we did have some questions about the 30 percent ownership. There are many small business owners that are small business owners but they have a little, larger than 30 percent ownership in another restaurant or another bar. And just because they do own another business, doesn’t mean that they’re not struggling to stay open at another location. So we’ll submit some additional comments, but again we think the streetscape of New York City is vital to keeping New York City the restaurant and nightlife capital of the world. And to do that, we need to know what’s going on 8in the streets so the bills that will help compile the list of vacancies and other related data wood certainly be helpful. So again, we’re supported of these bills, and we think the council needs to act quickly, and we hope that the Diblazio administration, particularly with the regulatory review panel is committed to making this happen. When he was then candidate for Mayor, he believed that this bill didn’t go far enough. So now that he is the Mayor, we hope that his bill goes farther than he had anticipated, and we provide cures for the countless violations issued to businesses that do not impact the public immediately.

turns.text: Good morning. This will begin the Small Business Commission Hearing. I d am Council Member Mark Gjonaj, Chair of the Committee of Small Business. I'd like to welcome you to our hearing on a package of nine bills that are designed to improve the environment for small business in our city. Thank you for making the time for us today. Mom and Pop shops frequently navigate in our [Inaudible-1:30] of thousands of rules and regulations as they set up their businesses. Building, sanitation and zoning codes can cost local entrepreneurs thousands of dollars in start up costs as well as months and even years of invaluable time. That's why I sponsored Intro 1467 which would create an interactive website that would provide businesses with information about applicable laws, rules, penalties and fines. It is absolutely vital that the small businesses can access and understand local regulation as swiftly as possible. In a similar vane, I am also proud to co- sponsor alongside my colleagues, Council Member Espinal and Yeger, Intro 1466 which would create a regulatory review panel that will view New York City's Regulatory Architecture in order to identify cure periods for certain violations. Another major area of concern that we have identified over the course of the last several years has been the issue of vacant store fronts. Two bills under considerations today will tackle the crisis head on by helping the city acquire a more holistic and comprehensive understanding of this problem. Intro 1472 sponsored by Council Members Rosenthal, Yeager and the Speaker will acquire a part in the small business services to maintain a data base of commercial properties while Intro 1473 sponsored by Council Members Rosenthal, Rivera, Kallos and the Speaker would require a registration of vacant store front property. Additionally, Council Members Rivera, the Speaker, Yeger and Presamble, Levine and Levin have introduced Intro 1089 which will require periodic surveys by SBS to assess the state of storefront businesses. We're also making efforts to facilitate the process by which local shops expand that small businesses are the life, blood and employment in the city. Roughly nine out every ten employers in New York City has fewer than 20 employees. However, it can be a daunting prospect to expand your services which is why Council Member Rosenthal, alongside the Speaker has introduced Intro 1471 which requires SBS to offer business assistance. Expansion, however, is not the only concern. Sometimes just keeping your location can be a struggle, so to protect local institutions from unscrupulous landlords, council members Levine, Rivera, Powers, Rosenthal and Ayala have introduced 1470 which will make low cost legal services available to small business owners who are facing eviction proceedings. Intro 1410, sponsored by Council Member Gibson has similar intention. This bill would require certification of no harassment before the approval of construction documents and demolition permits for commercial buildings. Lastly, we are seeking to address the issue of affordability. Intro 1408 by Council Members Espinal, Combo and Chin would establish a requirement for affordable retail space, and all development projects that receive city assistance. I could not be more proud to hold a hearing on such an exciting package of legislation. We want small businesses in New York City to be able to expand swiftly, comply with regulations easily and address logistical and legal challenges with as little fuss as possible. Taken together, these bills will provide vital support for Mom and Pop shops in a highly competitive and challenging client. I'd like to thank the Committee Staff, Council Irene Bosky, Policy Analyst Michael Kirtz as well as my Chief of Staff, Reggie Johnson, for making this hearing possible. Finally, I'd like to recognize the committee members that have joined us, and many more will, Council Members Ayala and Council Member Gibson.
